title: Ontario Home Cooks Share Family Diwali Recipes in Free Community Cookbook
excerpt: Food Basics' first More Flavours of Home edition features Scarborough's Vibha Ajwani and Kitchener-Waterloo's Harinder Dhaliwal, whose recipes were learned at family stoves, not written down.
body:
• Food Basics has launched More Flavours of Home, a free community-sourced cookbook whose first edition collects Diwali recipes from Ontario residents.
  • Scarborough home cook Vibha Ajwani contributes Kesar Shrikhand, a saffron and cardamom yogurt dessert central to her family's Diwali.
  • Harinder Dhaliwal of Kitchener-Waterloo contributes Aloo Parantha, a spiced potato flatbread learned from her mother-in-law and unchanged for years.
  • The cookbook is available free at foodbasics.ca/more-flavours, with ingredients stocked in Food Basics stores across Ontario.

Genuine Indian home cooking is coming out of Ontario kitchens and into print this Diwali. Food Basics has launched the first edition of More Flavours of Home, a community-sourced cookbook built from recipes that, as the retailer notes, are often never written down at all — learned at a family member's side and measured by a handful of this and a pinch of that.

Following nominations from across the province, two home cooks anchor the Diwali edition: Vibha Ajwani of Scarborough and Harinder Dhaliwal of Kitchener-Waterloo, selected, according to YourCityWithIN, not only for their cooking but for their engagement with their communities.

Two recipes, two family histories

Ajwani, who blends traditional and modern Indian cooking, contributes her Kesar Shrikhand — a creamy dessert enriched with saffron, cardamom and sugar that holds a special place in her family's Diwali celebrations. In her kitchen, Food Basics says, there is always a festival on the horizon, and every recipe is a way to keep family traditions alive across generations.

Dhaliwal's contribution is savoury: Aloo Parantha, a flatbread made from scratch and stuffed with a spiced potato blend. She demonstrated the dish live at an exhibition ahead of the cookbook's release.

"These are recipes that I learned from family, and this one specifically, from my mother-in-law. I married into a big family, and what we prepared as a result was soul food."

— Harinder Dhaliwal, home cook, Kitchener-Waterloo

Dhaliwal told YourCityWithIN the recipe stands completely unchanged today: "We've been doing it for years, and it is how my kids grew up eating, and beyond that, how their relatives and friends ate as well." Every morning, she said, you get your rolling pin and get to work — the food has to feed everyone, kids and adults.

Why it matters beyond the recipes

Food Basics vice president Hardeep Kharaud emphasised that many cherished recipes are unwritten, passed down through family experience — which is precisely what the cookbook series is trying to capture before those measurements-by-handful disappear. The launch announcement, carried by GlobeNewswire, describes the edition as a celebration of the residents and families who keep cultural traditions alive through food.

For diaspora readers in the Greater Toronto Area, the practical path is simple: the cookbook is available free at foodbasics.ca/more-flavours, and Food Basics says the ingredients are readily accessible in its stores across Ontario — in time for this weekend's Diwali celebrations.
